clinical_targets.goal: Slow annual eGFR decline to < 1–2 mL/min/1.73m²/year
Improvement in peak flow rate (Qmax > 15 mL/s) and IPSS reduction ≥ 4 points

steps_summary: Step 1: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
Step 2: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
Step 3: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
Step 4: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care

steps.title: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
steps.rationale: Initial management of Kidney Diseases focuses on non-pharmacological foundations, patient education, elimination of precipitating triggers, and initiating evidence-based first-line monotherapy. Treatment should begin at the lowest effective dose with periodic reassessment.

drug_classes.role: Standard initial therapy for mild-to-moderate Kidney Diseases.
drug_classes.dosing: Initiate standard therapeutic dosing; titrate over 2–4 weeks based on clinical response and tolerability.
drug_classes.pearls: Monitor for early therapeutic response; assess patient compliance and verify baseline organ function.

steps.title: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
steps.rationale: For patients with persistent symptoms, partial response, or disease progression after 4–8 weeks of Step 1 therapy, escalate by titrating to the maximum tolerated dose or adding a complementary second-line agent with a distinct mechanism of action.

drug_classes.role: Dose optimization and complementary therapeutic escalation.
drug_classes.dosing: Titrate to target clinical biomarker thresholds under specialist guidance.
drug_classes.pearls: Evaluate patient compliance and consider secondary causes of treatment resistance.

steps.title: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
steps.rationale: Patients with severe, recalcitrant, or treatment-refractory Kidney Diseases require multidisciplinary subspecialist evaluation and consideration of advanced therapies (biologics, targeted small molecules, immunosuppressive regimens, or specialized combination protocols).

drug_classes.role: Multidisciplinary tertiary intervention for refractory disease.
drug_classes.pearls: Consult subspecialty guidelines and consider therapeutic drug monitoring where applicable.

steps.title: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care
steps.rationale: Reserved for treatment-resistant, acute progressive, or complicated disease. Protocol includes parenteral salvage therapies, procedural or surgical interventions, inpatient stabilization, and long-term rehabilitation.

drug_classes.role: Rescue intervention for complicated or refractory Kidney Diseases.
drug_classes.dosing: Hospital or tertiary center procedural protocol.
drug_classes.pearls: Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

special_populations.renal_impairment: Individualize drug dosing based on calculated CrCl (Cockcroft-Gault) or eGFR.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Monitor for altered drug-protein binding in hypoalbuminemic nephrotic states.
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: RAAS inhibitors are contraindicated; labetalol, nifedipine, or methyldopa are preferred for hypertension.
special_populations.elderly: Watch for orthostatic hypotension with alpha-1 blockers (tamsulosin) in elderly men.

style_3_monograph.summary: You have two kidneys, each about the size of your fist. They are near the middle of your back, just below the rib cage. Inside each kidney there are about a million tiny structures called nephrons. They filter your blood. They remove wastes and extra water, which become urine. The urine flows through tubes called ureters. It goes to your bladder, which stores the urine until you go to the bathroom. Most kidney diseases attack the nephrons. This damage may leave kidneys unable to remove wastes. Causes can include genetic problems, injuries, or medicines. You have a higher risk of kidney disease if you have diabetes , high blood pressure , or a close family member with kidney disease. Chronic kidney disease damages the nephrons slowly over several years. Other kidney problems include: Cancer Cysts Stones Infections Your doctor can do blood and urine tests to check if you have kidney disease. If your kidneys fail , you will need dialysis or a kidney transplant . NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases
style_3_monograph.treatment: Some people do not need treatment. Blood clots may get better on their own over time. You may have treatment to open the artery if the blockage is discovered quickly or it is affecting your only working kidney. Treatment to open the artery may include: Clot-dissolving medicines (thrombolytics) Medicines that prevent the blood from clotting (anticoagulants), such as warfarin Surgical repair of the renal artery Insertion of a tube (catheter) into the renal artery to open the blockage You may need temporary dialysis to treat acute kidney failure. Medicines to lower cholesterol may be needed if the blockage is due to clots from plaque buildup in the arteries.
